title: Mindfulness training for stress
description: Mindfulness training, such as the 8-week Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction course, teaches people to pay attention to the present moment without judging it, through meditation and gentle movement. Trials compared it with other training of the same length. Afterwards, the right amygdala reacted less to positive pictures and worked more closely with an area at the front of the brain involved in regulating emotion. Brightness and lines show the change since before training: violet means less than before, a pulsing line means working together more, a dashed line less.
caveat: The findings come from two randomised trials, one of an 8-week course in healthy, non-clinical adults and one of a 3-day intensive course in stressed unemployed adults, and a review of 26 brain-imaging studies. The amygdala reacted less to positive pictures, but not to negative ones, after the 8-week course. The review reports increases in "activity, connectivity and volume" in several areas together, without separating them, so those are described, not drawn. These are not studies of an illness: it is linked to Acute stress, but the trials studied everyday or ongoing stress, not acute stress. The first part is drawn at rest. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.

phases.name: Before treatment
phases.caption: Before training. The comparison here starts from each person's own level, so the brain is drawn at rest.

phases.name: Mindfulness training
phases.caption: An 8-week course in one trial, a 3-day intensive retreat in the other. People were not scanned during this time.

citations.authors: Kral TRA, Schuyler BS, Mumford JA, Rosenkranz MA, Lutz A, Davidson RJ
citations.title: Impact of short- and long-term mindfulness meditation training on amygdala reactivity to emotional stimuli.
citations.quote: Short-term training consisted of an 8-week Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction course (N=32, 22 female), which was compared to an active control condition (N=35, 19 female) in a randomized controlled trial.

citations.authors: Taren AA, Gianaros PJ, Greco CM, Lindsay EK, Fairgrieve A, Brown KW, Rosen RK, et al.
citations.title: Mindfulness meditation training alters stress-related amygdala resting state functional connectivity: a randomized controlled trial.
citations.quote: Consistent with this prediction, a flexible factorial random effects analysis showed that a 3-day intensive mindfulness meditation training program reduced right amygdala-sgACC (MNI: 0, 18, −12) rsFC, compared with relaxation training without a mindfulness component (time × treatment interaction P < 0.05, k = 28, corrected for multiple comparisons) (Table 3, Figure 3).

phases.name: What changed
phases.caption: After training, the right amygdala reacts less to positive pictures and works more closely with the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, which helps regulate emotion. After a 3-day course, the right amygdala works less closely with the subgenual cingulate at rest, a link that is stronger in people under more stress.

phases.caption: After the 8-week course, reactions to negative pictures did not change; the authors suggest that may need more practice. The left amygdala's links did not change after the 3-day course.

order.rationale: This last part is a summary of what the studies did not find or did not measure, not a later point in time.

regions.explanation: The right amygdala reacted less to positive pictures after an 8-week mindfulness course than after a control course, in one trial; no difference for negative pictures. A review of mindfulness studies also describes decreased amygdala activity.
